answer.generated: Main-memory database systems ensure transactional integrity during long-duration transactions through multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), which contrasts fundamentally with traditional locking mechanisms. MVCC allows transactions to read a snapshot of the database state as it existed at the start of the transaction, thus enabling concurrent access without blocking other transactions. This approach avoids the overhead and contention associated with traditional locking, where transactions must wait for locks to be released before proceeding. In contrast, locking mechanisms typically employ row-level or table-level locks to manage access, which can lead to significant blocking and serialization of transactions, especially in scenarios with high concurrency. MVCC achieves this by maintaining multiple versions of data items, each visible to transactions based on their start time. For example, a transaction initiated at time t1 can read a version of data from time t0, while another transaction starting at t2 can read a different version of the same data from time t1. This method ensures that long-duration transactions do not impede short transactions and maintains a consistent view of the database across all concurrently running transactions, thereby enhancing both performance and scalability in main-memory environments.
